title: Consumer Rights
subject: economics
syllabus_note: Follows the CBSE 2025-26 Social Science (087) syllabus: Consumer Rights is project work only (internally assessed) and is not evaluated in the board examination. This lesson supports the project. The pecuniary limits of consumer commissions follow the 2021 rules under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019; the NCERT book may print older limits.

blocks.title: An expired packet
blocks.body:
You buy a packet of biscuits and find, at home, that it is past its expiry date. Another time, a shopkeeper charges you more than the printed price, or a new scooter's brakes fail. What can you do?

Every one of us is a **consumer**. This chapter explains how consumers can be exploited, how the consumer movement grew in India, what our rights are, and where we can go for justice. **Note:** in 2025-26 this chapter is for the **project work** (Consumer Rights), not for the board examination.

blocks.title: Consumers have rights
blocks.body:
On **15 March 1962**, US President **John F. Kennedy** told the US Congress that consumers have basic rights, including the right to safety, the right to be informed, the right to choose and the right to be heard. This idea spread around the world.

Today, **15 March** is observed as **World Consumer Rights Day**. In India, **24 December** is **National Consumers' Day**, the day the Consumer Protection Act was passed in **1986**.
blocks.future: This chapter leads to careers in consumer law, quality control, standards testing, journalism and public administration.

blocks.question: Why might a consumer be cheated more easily by a big company than by a neighbour who sells goods?
options: Because big companies have more information, power and money than an individual consumer
Because big companies always sell bad goods
blocks.explanation: When producers are few and powerful, and consumers lack information, exploitation becomes easier.

blocks.title: Why rules are needed and how the consumer movement grew
blocks.body:
**Consumers in the marketplace:** we participate in the market both as **producers** and as **consumers**. As consumers, we buy goods and services for final use. Individual consumers often find themselves in a **weak position**: whenever there is a complaint about a good or service, the seller tries to shift the responsibility to the buyer, as if the seller has no responsibility once the sale is complete.

**Ways in which consumers are exploited:**
- **Weighing less** than they should, or **adding extra charges**.
- **Adulteration** (for example, of edible oil, butter and ghee) and **defective goods**.
- **Selling expired goods** or charging more than the **maximum retail price (MRP)**.
- **False or incomplete information** in advertisements, and **poor after-sales service**.

**Factors that cause exploitation:** **limited information** with consumers; **limited supplies**, which lead to hoarding and black marketing; **limited competition**, when one or a few producers control the market; and **low literacy**, which makes consumers unaware of their rights.

**Why rules and regulations are needed:** markets do not always work in a fair manner. Large companies with huge wealth, power and reach can manipulate the market in various ways, and false information is passed on through the media to attract consumers. Rules and regulations are required to **protect consumers**. For example, a company may sell a product for years even when it is known to be harmful; rules make companies take responsibility.

**The consumer movement in India:** it arose out of **dissatisfaction** of consumers, as many unfair practices were being indulged in by sellers.
- In the **1960s**, there was rampant **food shortage, hoarding, black marketing and adulteration** of food and edible oil. This gave birth to the consumer movement in an **organised form**.
- Till the 1970s, consumer organisations were largely engaged in **writing articles** and holding **exhibitions**. They formed **consumer groups** to look into the malpractices in ration shops and overcrowding in road passenger transport.
- In **1986**, the Indian government enacted the **Consumer Protection Act (COPRA)**. This was a major step. It has now been replaced by the **Consumer Protection Act, 2019**.
- **Consumers International:** in **1985**, the United Nations adopted the **UN Guidelines for Consumer Protection**. Consumers International (earlier the International Organisation of Consumers Unions) has become an umbrella body of over **200 member organisations** from more than **100 countries**, including India.

options: full and correct information with consumers
blocks.explanation: Well-informed consumers are harder to cheat.

blocks.explanation: It has been replaced by the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.
option_feedback: That is Kennedy's speech on consumer rights.

blocks.title: The rights of consumers
blocks.body:
**1. Right to safety:** consumers have the right to be protected against the marketing of goods and delivery of services that are **hazardous to life and property**. Many goods and services, such as pressure cookers, electrical appliances, cars and medicines, need special attention to safety. Producers must follow **safety rules and regulations**.

**2. Right to be informed:** when we buy a commodity, we find details given on the packing: **ingredients, price, batch number, date of manufacture, expiry date and address** of the manufacturer. When we buy medicines, we find 'directions for proper use' and information on side effects. Consumers have the right to be informed about the particulars of the goods and services they buy, so that they can **complain and ask for compensation** if the product proves defective. If a seller charges more than the **MRP** printed on the packet, consumers can protest and complain.
- The **Right to Information (RTI) Act**, passed in **October 2005**, ensures citizens all the information about the functions of **government departments**.

**3. Right to choose:** any consumer who receives a service, in whatever capacity, regardless of age, gender and nature of service, has the right to **choose** whether to continue to receive the service. Sometimes we are **forced** to buy things we do not want: for example, a gas supply dealer may insist that you buy a **gas stove** from him when you take a new connection. This denies the right to choose.

**4. Right to seek redressal:** consumers have the right to seek redressal against **unfair trade practices and exploitation**. If any damage is done to a consumer, she has the right to get **compensation** depending on the degree of damage.

**5. Right to represent:** consumers have the right to be represented in the **consumer protection councils** and to be heard. The Act has enabled consumers to have this right.

**6. Right to consumer education:** consumers should know their rights and be able to use them. Schools have **consumer clubs**, and the government uses media campaigns such as **'Jago Grahak Jago'** to spread awareness.

**Duties of consumers (taking part):** check the **quality and price**, look for **standard marks**, ask for a **bill** (cash memo) for every purchase, read the **expiry date**, and **complain** about genuine grievances. Consumers can also express **solidarity** by forming **consumer groups and voluntary organisations**.

blocks.title: Rights of consumers
blocks.body:
| Right | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Right to safety** | protection against goods and services that are hazardous to life and property | a pressure cooker with a faulty safety valve can cause a serious accident |
| **Right to be informed** | information about ingredients, price (MRP), batch number, date of manufacture, expiry date and address of the maker | checking the expiry date on medicines |
| **Right to choose** | freedom to choose among goods and services; no forced purchase | a gas dealer cannot insist that you buy a stove with a new connection |
| **Right to seek redressal** | compensation for unfair trade practices and exploitation | getting a refund or replacement for a defective product |
| **Right to represent** | to be heard in consumer protection bodies | consumer representatives in consumer protection councils |
| **Right to consumer education** | to learn about rights and how to use them | consumer clubs in schools |

blocks.question: A dealer insists that you buy a gas stove from him to get a new gas connection. Which right is denied?
blocks.explanation: Consumers must be free to choose what they buy.
option_feedback: This is about forced purchase, not danger.
This is about being heard in councils.

sections.title: Where to go for justice, and standard marks

blocks.title: Consumer commissions and standardisation
blocks.body:
**Consumer commissions:** under the Consumer Protection Act, a **three-tier quasi-judicial machinery** has been set up at the **district, state and national levels** to settle consumer disputes. These bodies are popularly called **consumer courts**.
- The **District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission** deals with cases involving claims up to **Rs 50 lakh** (as per the 2021 rules under the 2019 Act).
- The **State Commission** deals with claims above Rs 50 lakh and up to **Rs 2 crore**.
- The **National Commission** in New Delhi deals with claims above **Rs 2 crore**.
- If a case is dismissed at the district level, the consumer can **appeal** in the State Commission and then in the National Commission.
- Consumers can file complaints themselves; they do not always need a lawyer. Consumer groups also **guide consumers** on how to file cases and often **represent** them.

**Standardisation of products:** standard marks help consumers be assured of quality while buying goods.
- **ISI mark:** given by the **Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS)** for industrial and consumer goods.
- **Agmark:** for **agricultural products** such as edible oil, cereals and honey.
- **Hallmark:** for **gold and silver jewellery**, certified by BIS.
- **ISO:** international standards for quality.
- For some products that affect the **health and safety** of consumers, such as **LPG cylinders, food colours and additives, cement and packaged drinking water**, it is **mandatory** for producers to get certified by these organisations.

**Progress of the consumer movement:** **24 December** is observed as **National Consumers' Day** in India, as COPRA was passed on this day in 1986. India has hundreds of consumer groups, but only a few are well organised. The redressal process is often **cumbersome, expensive and time-consuming**; many consumers do not keep bills, and laws are not always enforced. So consumers need to be **aware and active**, and the movement needs voluntary effort and participation of all.

blocks.title: Three-tier consumer commissions
blocks.body:
| Level | Called | Value of claims it hears (2021 rules) |
|---|---|---|
| **District level** | District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission | up to Rs 50 lakh |
| **State level** | State Commission | above Rs 50 lakh up to Rs 2 crore |
| **National level** | National Commission (New Delhi) | above Rs 2 crore |

blocks.question: Which mark would you look for on a bottle of honey?
blocks.explanation: Agmark certifies agricultural products such as honey, edible oil and cereals.
option_feedback: ISO is an international quality standard, but Agmark certifies agricultural produce like honey.

blocks.question: A consumer court at the district level is called the:
blocks.explanation: It is the first level of the three-tier system.
option_feedback: Consumer cases go to consumer commissions.

blocks.title: Memory tricks
blocks.body:
- **Six rights "S-I-C-R-R-E"**: Safety, Information, Choice, Redressal, Representation, Education.
- **Exploitation factors "Info, Supply, Competition, Literacy"** (all limited/low).
- **Dates: COPRA 1986 (24 December = National Consumers' Day); CPA 2019; RTI 2005; 15 March = World Consumer Rights Day.**
- **Marks: ISI = industry, Agmark = agriculture, Hallmark = jewellery.**
- **Three tiers: District → State → National.**

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.body:
1. Using Hallmark for honey: honey and edible oil carry **Agmark**; Hallmark is for **jewellery**.
2. Saying consumer courts are ordinary criminal courts: they are **quasi-judicial consumer commissions**.
3. Mixing up National Consumers' Day (**24 December**, India) with World Consumer Rights Day (**15 March**).
4. Thinking a consumer must pay more than MRP: charging **above MRP** is unfair and can be challenged.
5. Forgetting that this chapter is for the **project**, not the board exam, in 2025-26.

blocks.title: Try this in class
blocks.body: Ask students to bring five empty packets (food, medicine, cosmetics). In groups, list the MRP, date of manufacture, expiry date, standard mark and customer care number on each. Discuss which right each item of information supports. This can start the consumer rights project.

blocks.title: Think and explain
blocks.body: Have you or your family ever been overcharged or sold a defective product? What did you do? Which consumer right could you have used?

blocks.title: Mastery challenge (project starter)
blocks.body:
'An aware consumer is a protected consumer.' Explain in about 120 words.

**Model answer:** Consumers are exploited through under-weighing, adulteration, defective goods, charging above MRP and misleading advertisements, mainly because of limited information, limited supplies, limited competition and low literacy. An aware consumer checks the MRP, ingredients, date of manufacture and expiry date, looks for standard marks such as ISI, Agmark and Hallmark, and asks for a bill. Such a consumer knows the rights to safety, information, choice, redressal, representation and education, and can approach the district, state or national consumer commission under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. Consumer groups help by guiding and representing consumers. Awareness therefore turns rights on paper into real protection.

blocks.title: Chapter summary
blocks.body:
- Consumers are often in a weak position and can be exploited through under-weighing, adulteration, defective goods, charging above MRP and false information.
- Exploitation is caused by limited information, limited supplies, limited competition and low literacy; rules are needed to protect consumers.
- The consumer movement grew from the 1960s; COPRA was enacted in 1986 and replaced by the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.
- Consumers have rights to safety, information, choice, redressal, representation and education; the RTI Act 2005 gives information about government work.
- Three-tier consumer commissions (district, state, national) settle disputes; ISI, Agmark and Hallmark assure quality.
- In 2025-26, this chapter is for project work, not the board exam.

blocks.title: Project tips
blocks.body:
- In 2025-26, Consumer Rights is one of the **project** options (internally assessed); it is **not** in the board examination.
- A good project includes a survey of packets and bills, a case study of a real consumer complaint, the six consumer rights with examples, and the three-tier redressal system.
- Keep the bills and photos of labels you collect as evidence in your project file.

blocks.back: Right to safety, to be informed, to choose, to seek redressal, to represent, and to consumer education.

blocks.back: ISI: industrial and consumer goods (BIS). Agmark: agricultural products. Hallmark: gold and silver jewellery.
